strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: automating the development of domain-specific scientific methods rather than merely assembling existing analysis tools.

TusoAI is presented as a coherent end-to-end system combining literature-derived instructions, diverse candidate generation, iterative evaluation, feedback, and diagnostics. The paper includes pseudocode and several prompt templates that help explain the approach.

The empirical scope is broad, covering six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, multiple LLM backbones, component ablations, and two genetics case studies. Evaluation on deployment datasets distinct from the optimization dataset is a particularly valuable design choice in the single-cell benchmarks.

Several results are promising, including strong average rank on the single-cell tasks, competitive scientific deep-learning performance, low reported inference/search costs with GPT-4o-mini, and interpretable modifications to scDRS and pgBoost.
weaknesses: The headline comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent receive only 2–10 iterations and sometimes substantially less than the nominal eight-hour budget; on deep-learning tasks they are replaced by the best of ten independently prompted models rather than comparable iterative agents. AIDE also uses different execution limits. The selected single-cell 'expert' baselines are chosen partly for efficiency and are not necessarily the strongest available methods, despite being described as top-performing. These discrepancies substantially weaken claims of state-of-the-art superiority.

There is serious evaluator-overfitting and possible leakage risk. Agents see executable evaluation code and operate on data objects that may contain targets—for example, the denoising template passes an AnnData object containing obsm['test'] directly to the generated function. The paper specifies no sandboxing, forbidden-field checks, held-out evaluator, or manual audit of final programs. Supplying final generated code would be necessary to verify that benchmark signals are not accessed or otherwise exploited.

The pgBoost case study appears to optimize enrichment against eQTL and ABC gold-standard links and then report improvement on those same resources, without a clearly held-out link, chromosome, or dataset split. Testing 511 feature combinations against the reported evaluation sets creates a substantial adaptive-overfitting risk. Likewise, the claimed seven 'novel' variant–gene links and nine new disease–cell associations receive no independent replication or functional validation; biological plausibility alone does not establish discovery.

The evidence is statistically weak for a highly stochastic search procedure. Most experiments use only three seeds, significance tests are absent, and uncertainty from selecting the best among many adaptively evaluated programs is not addressed. Figure 5 shows especially large run-to-run variation for decomposition, while the main text states that all confidence intervals are below 0.01 without adequately reconciling this instability.

The ablations cover only five of eleven tasks, provide no uncertainty estimates, and do not cleanly support every claimed component: removing diagnosis has the same reported average rank as the full system and improves several individual results, while some alternative LLM backbones outperform the default. The multiplicative 1.1 category-weight update is also described as 'Bayesian' without a probabilistic model or posterior update.

The deep-learning results do not establish broad superiority: TusoAI is not best on NinaPro, ECG, or DeepSEA, and its mean score is slightly below DARTS, despite having the best reported mean rank. Task and metric selection is also partly post hoc, including excluding half of NAS-Bench-360 and changing the SVG metric from the benchmark's original correlation measure.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central claims. The manuscript's code-availability URL is blank, final discovered programs and complete optimization prompts are omitted, and important details such as code clustering, exact model/API versions, token and evaluation budgets, data-access restrictions, and per-baseline compute are insufficiently specified. Overall, the idea and preliminary results are interesting, but the current evaluation does not reliably support the claimed scientific-method and biological-discovery advances.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: using LLM agents to develop domain-specific scientific methods rather than merely assemble existing analysis tools.
The evaluation is unusually broad, covering six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, several LLM backbones, component ablations, and two genetics case studies.
The use of separate optimization and deployment datasets in the main benchmarks is a good design choice, and the reported single-cell results are promising.

The paper provides useful implementation detail through pseudocode, prompt templates, example instructions, runtime limits, and cost measurements. The resulting scDRS and pgBoost modifications are also concise and interpretable.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not sufficiently controlled. TusoAI receives an eight-hour optimization budget, whereas Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent run for variable and often much shorter periods; AIDE uses a different execution timeout; and the deep-learning GPT-5/Claude baselines are only the best of ten independently generated models. Compute, calls, tokens, hardware, and optimization opportunities are not matched.

The claimed comparison with a “top-performing expert” is misleading. Appendix E states that the single-cell expert was selected from the top three partly for runtime efficiency, rather than selecting the actual strongest method. TusoAI also does not consistently beat the best method on the deep-learning tasks and has a lower mean score than DARTS, making several superiority claims too broad.

The proposed technical machinery is modest and sometimes inaccurately characterized. The purported Bayesian update is simply a 1.1 multiplicative increase after a successful proposal, with no posterior, uncertainty model, or principled treatment of failures. The knowledge tree is largely prompt organization, while diagnosis and diversity selection are underspecified.

Statistical support does not capture the principal source of variance: the stochastic agent search. The main confidence intervals appear to concern three training seeds for selected solutions. Appendix F shows only validation outcomes from three agent runs and reveals severe instability for decomposition, including a negative run, but deployment performance across independent searches is not reported. Significance tests are absent.

The ablations cover only five of eleven tasks, report no uncertainty, and do not cleanly establish every claimed contribution. In particular, removing diagnosis has the same average rank as the full system and improves three of the five reported task scores.

The benchmark construction leaves substantial researcher discretion: only subsets of both benchmark suites are retained, some standard metrics are removed or replaced, scores are custom-normalized, and expert baselines are manually selected. Sensitivity to these choices and complete per-dataset results are not provided.

The pgBoost case study has a serious apparent evaluation-leakage problem. TusoAI directly optimizes enrichment against eQTL and ABC gold-standard links, then reports improvements on those same types of benchmarks without describing held-out links, chromosomes, or datasets. The reported gains therefore need not reflect generalization.

The “novel biology” claims are not adequately validated. Newly called disease–cell and variant–gene associations receive only post hoc literature plausibility arguments, without independent cohorts, orthogonal assays, preregistered hypotheses, or experimental confirmation. Calling them discoveries is stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: final generated methods, exact task-specific prompts and retrieved paper sets, complete candidate trajectories, per-run results, and sufficient configurations to reconstruct all comparisons are not included. Overall, the promising empirical signal is insufficiently controlled to support the paper’s central claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: TusoAI addresses an important and timely problem: autonomously developing domain-specific scientific methods rather than merely assembling existing analysis tools. The combination of literature-derived knowledge trees, diverse candidate maintenance, iterative execution, and diagnostic feedback is coherent and practically motivated.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, multiple LLM backbones, component ablations, and two genetics case studies. Using separate optimization and deployment datasets for the main benchmarks is a meaningful safeguard against direct validation-set overfitting.

Results are generally competitive and sometimes compelling. TusoAI obtains the best average rank on both benchmark groups, substantially improves several single-cell tasks, and produces concise, interpretable modifications to scDRS and pgBoost rather than only opaque model ensembles.

The paper includes useful behavioral analyses of search trajectories, code diversity, computational cost, and backbone sensitivity. The finding that inexpensive, low-latency models can work well within a structured agent framework is practically significant.
The manuscript is clear and well organized, and the genetics applications demonstrate potential scientific utility beyond benchmark-score optimization.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is not sufficiently controlled. TusoAI receives eight hours per task, whereas Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent run for varying durations and numbers of iterations; for deep-learning tasks they are replaced by the best of ten one-shot LLM proposals. AIDE also retains a different execution timeout. These differences make it difficult to attribute gains to the proposed architecture rather than compute, interaction budget, or implementation conditions.

The claimed comparison with top expert methods is overstated. For the single-cell tasks, the paper deliberately selects efficient methods such as logistic regression, ComBat, NNLS, and t-SNE from among the top three eligible methods, rather than consistently comparing with the strongest available application-specific approach. On the deep-learning suite, TusoAI is competitive but does not consistently beat task-specific methods and wins outright on relatively few tasks.

Uncertainty estimates do not capture the main source of variance. Reported confidence intervals appear to come from retraining selected solutions with three seeds, rather than rerunning the stochastic eight-hour discovery process. Figure 5 indicates substantial between-run instability for some tasks, but agent-level replicated test results and statistical comparisons are absent.

The ablations are limited to five tasks, apparently without repeated agent runs or uncertainty estimates. Some results do not cleanly support the stated component-level conclusions: removing diagnosis ties the default average rank and improves multiple individual tasks. Moreover, the so-called Bayesian update is only a multiplicative reward after improvement, without an explicit probabilistic model, uncertainty representation, or negative evidence; describing it as Bayesian is technically misleading.

The pgBoost case study does not clearly separate the gold-standard links used to guide the 511-step feature search from those used for final evaluation. Without held-out chromosomes, loci, or independent link sets, the reported enrichment gains may reflect adaptive overfitting. Similarly, the claims of seven previously unreported variant-gene links and nine new disease-cell associations require a systematic novelty assessment and independent biological validation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not provide the final discovered implementations, complete prompts for several central agents, exact search traces, token/API budgets, or sufficiently detailed configurations for all baselines. The displayed public-code link is also blank in the submitted PDF. These omissions make the headline results difficult to independently verify.

Several benchmark choices weaken comparability: the authors select only subsets of the source benchmarks, modify some official metrics, and summarize heterogeneous task scores by unweighted averages. These choices are sometimes reasonable, but sensitivity analyses using the complete or official evaluation protocols are needed.

Overall, the work is promising and potentially impactful, but the fairness of the agent comparisons, discovery-level statistical reliability, and possible leakage in the strongest biological case study prevent the evaluation from being convincing enough for acceptance at present.

strengths: TusoAI addresses an important and timely problem: automatically developing domain-specific scientific methods, rather than merely assembling workflows from existing tools.

The framework contains several sensible components, including literature-derived knowledge trees, diverse candidate maintenance, category-conditioned optimization, feedback, and data-driven diagnostics.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, multiple LLM backbones, component ablations, runtime and cost analyses, and three warm-start case studies.

Held-out deployment datasets are used for the single-cell tasks, while the NASBench-360 experiments retain predefined training, validation, and test splits. This is substantially stronger than reporting only optimization-set performance.
TusoAI performs strongly on the single-cell benchmark, obtaining the best average score and rank, and remains competitive across heterogeneous deep-learning tasks.
The paper provides useful analyses of optimization trajectories, generated-code diversity, literature quantity, prompt-summary length, LLM choice, and agent cost.

The scDRS and pgBoost case studies demonstrate practical compatibility with established scientific codebases and produce concise, interpretable modifications rather than only opaque generated pipelines.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix supplies algorithms, task definitions, prompts, baseline configurations, and evaluation details.
weaknesses: The reported uncertainty does not capture the most important source of variability: stochastic agent search. Main-table confidence intervals are primarily over downstream data splits or training seeds after selecting a method. Only three agent runs are shown for the single-cell tasks, and these reveal substantial instability for decomposition; comparable search-level replication is missing for deep-learning tasks and case studies.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. TusoAI receives eight hours, whereas Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent run for variable and often shorter durations; AIDE retains a different one-hour execution timeout because matched settings caused crashes; and the deep-learning substitutes are the best of ten one-shot generations. Consequently, the comparison mixes different compute budgets, interaction protocols, and selection procedures.

The deep-learning evidence is weaker than the narrative suggests. TusoAI has an average score of 0.70 versus 0.71 for DARTS, is clearly best on only Satellite, and is below task-specific or NAS baselines on several tasks. The claim of consistently superior performance should therefore be qualified.

The ablations do not cleanly establish every proposed component. Removing diagnostics has essentially the same average rank as the full system and improves some tasks, while effects vary substantially across tasks. Statistical comparisons across independent agent runs are absent.

Calling the simple 1.1 multiplicative category-weight update 'Bayesian' is misleading: no probabilistic model, posterior, uncertainty estimate, or derivation is provided. More principled bandit or search baselines would help establish whether this heuristic matters.

Task and metric selection introduces possible favorable-selection bias. Only subsets of OpenProblems and NASBench-360 are evaluated based partly on runtime and implementation convenience, and the SVG metric is changed from the benchmark's correlation measure to classification accuracy. Results on the complete feasible suite or a preregistered selection rule would be more convincing.

Benchmark contamination is a significant concern: the LLMs may have encountered the public benchmarks, methods, and repositories during pretraining, while TusoAI explicitly retrieves highly cited papers about the tasks. There are no temporally held-out tasks, newly constructed problems, or controls separating retrieval/reimplementation from genuine method discovery.

The novelty analysis of generated methods is largely qualitative. Several highlighted results combine familiar components such as NMF, coordinate regression, ResNet fine-tuning, augmentation, and ensembling. Comparisons against stronger hand-designed combinations or conventional AutoML/hyperparameter optimization are needed to show that agentic scientific reasoning is responsible for the gains.

The genetics case studies do not yet justify the strong claim of discovering 'new biology.' The reported findings are computational associations, often supported by existing literature, without independent prospective or experimental validation. For pgBoost, improvement and discovery are also assessed through closely related enrichment criteria, leaving overfitting concerns.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript itself: the advertised code URL is blank, final generated implementations are not provided, exact model snapshots and sampling settings are unclear, and some compute descriptions are inconsistent. Dependence on changing proprietary web agents further complicates reproduction.

The system optimizes a supplied scalar evaluator and is therefore vulnerable to evaluator exploitation and validation overfitting. The paper notes this limitation but does not provide systematic safeguards, adversarial checks, or an analysis of failed or invalid solutions.

strengths: The problem—automating domain-specific scientific method development—is important, timely, and potentially high-impact.

The evaluation spans 11 tasks across single-cell analysis and scientific deep learning, with additional genetics case studies, runtime analysis, optimization trajectories, and several component and backbone ablations.
The knowledge-tree organization, diversity-aware candidate selection, diagnostic iterations, and literature-conditioned prompting form a coherent practical system.
The manuscript is generally readable and the principal tables and figures communicate the reported results clearly.
weaknesses: Evaluator isolation is not established. Most concerningly, the supplied denoising template passes the entire AnnData object, including the held-out target in `adata.obsm["test"]`, into the function being optimized. Generated code could therefore access or modify the target. The paper itself reports that AIDE modified an evaluator on another task, demonstrating that such failures occur, yet it documents no sandboxing, access controls, or systematic audit of TusoAI outputs. This threatens the validity of central benchmark results.

The baseline comparison is not controlled fairly. Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent receive only 2–10 iterations over roughly 10 minutes to 5 hours, while TusoAI receives eight hours. Their deep-learning substitutes are the best of only ten direct LLM generations. AIDE retains a one-hour execution timeout because matching TusoAI's timeout caused crashes. These materially different search budgets and interfaces make the headline superiority difficult to interpret.

The claimed “top-performing expert” single-cell baselines are selected from the top three partly for runtime below ten minutes, rather than using the strongest available method. This weakens the assertion that TusoAI surpasses state-of-the-art expert algorithms.

Search uncertainty and selection effects are inadequately handled. Hundreds of validation-guided attempts are followed by reporting one selected solution; three downstream training seeds do not quantify variability across independent agent searches. The main tables omit independent search replicates, statistical tests, and correction for extensive adaptive model selection.

The ablations cover only five selected tasks and often show mixed evidence: removing diagnosis ties the default average rank and improves several individual tasks, while alternative LLMs outperform the default on average. No uncertainty is reported in the main ablation table, so several mechanistic claims are stronger than the evidence.

The two genetics studies do not convincingly establish new biological discovery. scDRS is optimized on one setting of the same simulation mechanism later used for evaluation, and its extra real-data associations receive literature-based plausibility rather than independent validation. pgBoost appears to optimize directly against eQTL and ABC enrichment and then evaluate improvements on those same gold-standard sources; no held-out links or datasets are described. The seven proposed links are defined by the optimized model's own percentile and are not experimentally or independently validated.

Methodological novelty is modest. The framework largely combines literature summarization, prompt-generated strategy lists, iterative code search, diagnostics, and heuristic reweighting. The multiplicative `π_c ← 1.1π_c` rule is called “Bayesian-style” but is not derived from a probabilistic model, ignores improvement magnitude and failures, and lacks comparison with standard bandit or search policies.

Claims that generated methods are novel are supported mainly by narrative comparisons. Several highlighted results, such as ResNet-50 fine-tuning with flips and rotations or combining standard preprocessing, losses, and ensembles, are conventional engineering choices. The final generated implementations are not included, preventing inspection for leakage, originality, correctness, or hidden library reuse.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The abstract says the code is publicly available “at” but provides no URL. Final generated methods, complete configurations, evaluator safeguards, retrieved papers and summaries, candidate histories, and exact per-run resource accounting are absent.

The algorithm specification contains inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 updates `Nsol`, which is otherwise unused, while candidate clustering and the changing number of retained solutions are insufficiently specified. Numerous consequential engineering choices are therefore not reproducible from the paper.

The broad claim of autonomously uncovering “new biology missed by existing methods” substantially exceeds the presented evidence. Overall, the potentially interesting system is undermined by evaluation leakage risk, unequal comparisons, weak independence of case-study validation, and missing reproducibility artifacts.

strengths: Clear and practically important contribution: an agentic framework for developing domain-specific scientific methods rather than merely composing existing tools.
Broad evaluation spanning six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, multiple LLM backbones, component ablations, optimization trajectories, and genetics case studies.
Optimization and testing are generally separated, mitigating validation-overfitting concerns.
Strong reported results, including the best average rank on both benchmark suites and substantial improvements over AIDE on most tasks.
Warm-start case studies demonstrate practical value by improving established genetics methods with concise, interpretable modifications.
Extensive prompt, runtime, cost, stability, and diversity analyses improve transparency.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: TusoAI receives eight hours, Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent often run for less time, deep-learning substitutes use the best of ten single-shot generations, and AIDE has a different execution timeout.

Some claims overstate the results. On deep-learning tasks, TusoAI's average score of 0.70 is below DARTS at 0.71 and only slightly above the expert baseline at 0.69, while trailing task-specific methods substantially on some tasks.

The single-cell benchmark is customized through task selection, metric changes, and use of an efficient top-three method as the 'expert' baseline rather than necessarily the strongest available method, creating selection-bias concerns.

Main confidence intervals do not adequately capture stochasticity from independent end-to-end agent searches. Repeated searches and paired significance tests are particularly important for small differences and ablations.

The methodological novelty is useful but heuristic. The so-called Bayesian update is a fixed multiplicative reward without a probabilistic model, negative updates, or theoretical justification; several other design choices lack sensitivity analysis.
Ablation evidence is mixed: removing diagnosis matches the default average rank and improves several tasks, weakening claims that every component is necessary.
The genetics results are promising computational hypotheses, but claims of uncovering 'new biology' are premature without independent experimental or prospective validation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: final generated methods are not included, the rendered manuscript lacks a usable code link, and compute, token, retrieval, and model-version details are not consistently reported across baselines.
